items.prompt: A milk depot in Otavi watches how the litres its farmers offer change whenever the farm-gate price changes. Define price elasticity of supply as the term applies to the depot's farmers.
items.canonical_answer: Price elasticity of supply measures how strongly the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer responds to a price change: the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price. Here: how far the farmers' litres respond to the farm-gate price.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: how strongly the quantity supplied responds to a change in price, measured as the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.
The meaning must tie the definition to the depot's litres; a definition of the demand-side measure alone earns nothing.

items.prompt: A worked-out figure for price elasticity of supply is a single number. Identify two features of this figure.
items.canonical_answer: It is a ratio of two percentage changes - quantity supplied over price - so it carries no units. And it is normally positive, because quantity supplied moves with price, and it is read against 1: above 1 is elastic supply, below 1 inelastic.
marking_guidance: Reward two characteristics of the figure, one mark each: a ratio of two percentage changes that carries no units; and a positive value read against 1 - above 1 elastic, below 1 inelastic.
What it includes: each feature must say what it involves, not just name it; restating the formula twice earns one mark.

items.prompt: Oshakati Textiles raised the price of its printed cotton from N$30 to N$36 a metre, a 20% rise, and the metres of cloth it offers each week rose from 500 to 750, a 50% rise. Define price elasticity of supply as the term applies to Oshakati Textiles' response.

marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.
The meaning must be tied to the mill's figures - the 50% rise in metres against the 20% price rise - rather than left as a formula alone.

items.prompt: A festival weekend raises the demand for fresh fish at the Walvis Bay Saturday market. The day's catch is already landed: at the old price of N$40 a kilo the market sold 300 kilos, and the new price settles at N$70 a kilo with 320 kilos sold. Discuss how a price-and-quantity diagram of this fish market shows what the elasticity of supply decided, giving a verbal walk-through of every part of the diagram and what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Price of fish (N$ a kilo) goes on the vertical axis and quantity (kilos) on the horizontal. The original demand curve D1 and supply curve S1 cross at E1: N$40 and 300 kilos. S1 is drawn steep, because the day's catch is already landed. The festival raises demand, so the whole demand curve shifts right to D2; supply does not shift, as no condition of supply changed, and the market moves up along S1. The new equilibrium E2, where D2 crosses S1, is at N$70 and 320 kilos. The diagram shows the shift landing mostly on price, up 70 - 40 = N$30 a kilo (75 per cent), and barely on quantity, up 320 - 300 = 20 kilos (under 7 per cent). The link is inelastic supply: with the catch fixed, sellers cannot follow the price. The consequence is that buyers carry the adjustment through a higher price; with a flatter supply curve the same demand shift would have raised quantity more and price less.
marking_guidance: The walk-through must name the axes labelled - price and quantity, each with its units - before anything else.
Reward the original curves drawn and labelled: D1 and S1 crossing at E1, at N$40 a kilo and 300 kilos, before the change is described.
Check the shift or movement, in the correct direction: the festival shifts demand right from D1 to D2 while supply holds, and the market moves along S1 - not the other way round.
The new equilibrium marked and labelled at E2, at N$70 and 320 kilos, and what the diagram shows, in words - the rise landing on price rather than on quantity - close the walk-through.
The link between the landed catch and the steepness of supply carries the analysis marks, and the consequence - buyers carrying the adjustment through a higher price - carries the evaluation.

items.prompt: Two firms worked out their supply elasticities for the past year. Namib Signs, a Katutura printing workshop: 2.8. Etosha Gate Lodge: 0.3. Explain what these figures show about how differently the two firms could respond to price changes.
items.canonical_answer: The figures show a sharp difference: Namib Signs' 2.8 is well above 1, so its supply is elastic, while Etosha Gate Lodge's 0.3 is well below 1, so its supply is inelastic. A 1% price rise brings 2.8% more printed work but only 0.3% more rooms. A printer can buy stock, run machines longer or hire within weeks, whereas a lodge cannot add rooms within a season. However, a lodge with closed rooms in the low season could respond more, and a printer at full capacity less.
marking_guidance: What the data shows - one figure far above 1 and one far below - must be stated first, with supporting evidence taken as a comparison of what each figure means.
The exception earns a mark: however, the lodge's figure may rise where spare rooms can be opened, and the printer's may fall once capacity is full and stores are empty.
The why - an explanation of the relationship between each business's setting and its responsiveness - is the core mark; quoting the two figures alone is not interpretation.

items.prompt: The price of a bag of milled maize at Gobabis rose from N$200 to N$240, a 20% rise. In the month that followed, the Gobabis maize mill offered 1 560 bags against 1 200 before, a 30% rise, and its supply elasticity worked out at 1.5. Explain what the figure of 1.5 shows about how the mill responded to the price change.
items.canonical_answer: Bags offered rose by 1 560 - 1 200 = 360, a 30% rise, against a 20% price rise, so PES = 30 / 20 = 1.5. Because quantity rose by a larger percentage than price, the mill's supply is elastic: it could follow the higher price with more output, probably by running longer shifts or drawing on stored grain. So the price rise was met with extra bags rather than a shortage, and the mill's buyers saw supply expand.
marking_guidance: The context - the 20% price rise beside the 360 extra bags - must anchor the answer, and the figures are the evidence.
Reasoning: because the percentage rise in quantity offered outstripped the percentage price rise, the link from price to output is what the 1.5 records.
Conclusion: therefore state what the figure means - elastic supply, extra bags meeting the demand - rather than restating the calculation.

items.prompt: A fishing tournament books out Ruacana for a season, and demand for rooms keeps rising. The town's lodges have 40 rooms each and no building can be finished within a season: room prices rise from N$1 200 to N$1 800 a night, and rooms let rise from 34 to 37 a night at the Ruacana River Lodge. Analyse what the elasticity of the lodges' supply means for the tournament's visitors, the lodge owners and the lodge workers.
items.canonical_answer: The tournament raises demand for rooms, but no lodge can be built within the season, so the supply of rooms is inelastic. The adjustment therefore falls mainly on price: the nightly rate rises by 1 800 - 1 200 = N$600, a 50 per cent rise, while rooms let at the River Lodge rise by only 37 - 34 = 3, under 9 per cent. Visitors pay N$600 a night more, and some may stay away. Lodge owners earn a higher rate on nearly the same rooms, so their takings rise without extra output. Workers serve almost the same number of guests on the same shifts, so they gain little until rooms, and hiring, can expand.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the season's demand rise against a fixed stock of rooms - must be named first, and an answer that starts from the price rise has the chain backwards.
Mechanism: because rooms cannot be added within a season, this causes supply to be inelastic, and the adjustment falls on price rather than on quantity.
Consequence: therefore each party needs its own traced outcome - the visitors, the lodge owners, the lodge workers - with the N$600 rise and the 3 extra rooms as the evidence.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands, including the workers left behind until rooms can be added.

items.prompt: State two determinants of price elasticity of supply.
items.canonical_answer: Any two of: spare capacity, the room to raise output without new equipment; the level of stocks of finished goods; the ease of switching production or finding extra inputs; and the length of time sellers have to respond.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise determinants: spare capacity, stocks, the ease of switching production or finding inputs, and the time period - one mark for each of any two.
The meaning of each must show it governs how far the quantity offered can respond, not the price itself.

items.prompt: Windhoek grows quickly and demand for bricks rises. The Katutura Brickworks is already firing its kilns flat out and its yard holds few finished bricks, while a newer yard outside the city has two kilns standing idle. Analyse how these differences between the two brickworks decide what happens to brick prices and brick output in the city.
items.canonical_answer: Rising demand for bricks meets two sellers in different conditions. Because spare capacity and stocks are determinants of PES, the newer yard's supply is elastic: it can light its idle kilns and raise output as prices rise. The Katutura Brickworks' supply is inelastic: its kilns are full and its yard nearly empty, so its output barely moves. So most of the city's extra demand is met by the newer yard, and the price rise is smaller than inelastic supply alone would bring. Builders pay less extra than otherwise; the newer yard and its workers gain trade and shifts; the Katutura Brickworks gets a higher price on unchanged output, more takings with no extra work for its crews.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the demand rise meeting two sellers with different spare capacity and stocks - must be named first.
Mechanism: because spare capacity and stock levels are determinants of supply elasticity, this causes one yard's supply to be elastic and the other's to be inelastic.
Consequence: therefore trace the outcome for prices and for each yard - extra bricks from the idle-kiln yard, and a smaller price rise than inelastic supply alone would have brought.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the builders, the two brickworks, the yard workers.

items.prompt: A sewing co-operative in Katutura holds a store of unprinted T-shirts and can buy cotton from two suppliers in the same week. A tailor in Oshakati sews made-to-order dresses from cloth bought once a month from a single fabric importer. Explain, using this extract, why the co-operative's supply is likely to be more elastic than the tailor's.
items.canonical_answer: The co-operative holds unprinted shirts in store and can buy cotton from two suppliers within a week, so it can turn a price rise into extra shirts within days. The tailor buys cloth once a month from one importer, so when her cloth runs out she cannot quickly make more, however much the price rises. Because stocks and easy access to inputs are determinants of PES, the co-operative's supply is likely to be the more elastic: quantity can follow price, while the tailor's output is tied to her monthly order.
marking_guidance: The context - the store of shirts and the two suppliers against the monthly cloth and the single importer - must anchor the answer, and the details of the extract are the evidence.
Reasoning: because stocks and access to inputs are determinants of elasticity, the link runs from each seller's conditions to how strongly the quantity offered can respond.
Conclusion: therefore state which supply is the more elastic and why, rather than naming determinants in the abstract.

items.prompt: The length of the period sellers have to respond is often called the most important influence on the elasticity of supply. Discuss whether the time period outweighs the other determinants.
items.canonical_answer: For the claim: in the very short run almost any seller's quantity is fixed by decisions already taken - a landed catch, a planted field, a full lodge - so supply is inelastic even for a seller with money and machines. Given months, the same seller can hire, build or plant, and spare capacity and stocks are themselves built up over time, so the period sets the ceiling on the other determinants. Against it: time is only the room in which the other determinants act. A mahangu field stays inelastic for the whole dry season, and a tailor with one fabric importer stays inelastic for a month however high the price climbs; meanwhile a seller with stored stock is elastic within the week, which is the stock, not time, at work. On balance, time matters most where sellers can change their capacity, stocks and inputs given time, and is outweighed where nature or a single supplier fixes them. What settles it is whether sellers' conditions can change within the period.
marking_guidance: Judgement: reward a stated position with a reason, not a fence-sit; on balance the best answers say why time sets the ceiling and where the claim fails.
Why it might: the argument for - the short run fixes quantity by decisions already taken, and the period sets the ceiling on every other determinant.
Why it might not: the argument against - time only matters where the other determinants have room to act, and examples where they do not, such as a dry season or a single importer, carry the mark.
Decisive: what settles it is whether sellers' other conditions can change within the time they have; answers naming that condition reach the top band.

items.prompt: Before planning for a season of higher demand, a Katutura furniture workshop works out the elasticity of its supply. Explain why the measure matters to the firm's planning.
items.canonical_answer: The elasticity of supply decides what a demand rise becomes. If the workshop's supply is elastic, extra demand becomes extra sales at close to the old price, because it can raise output. If supply is inelastic, the same rise shows up mainly as a higher price on nearly the same output, with customers turned away to rivals. Because workers, timber and shifts must be arranged before the season, the measure acts as a forecast: it tells the workshop whether to plan for more output or a higher price.
marking_guidance: Reward the reason: the elasticity of supply sets whether extra demand becomes extra output or a higher price on the same output.
Because elastic supply means the firm can meet demand with more units, and inelastic supply means demand lands on price and on customers turned away, each link needs to be made for the mark.
The purpose - a forecast for planning workers, timber and shifts - completes the reason.

items.prompt: The council of a growing town wants more houses built and offers builders a subsidy for each new home. In the town, builders hold no idle land, skilled bricklayers are scarce and building materials arrive on a single rail line. Explain, using this extract, what the elasticity of the town's housing supply suggests about the subsidy's first years.
items.canonical_answer: With no idle land, scarce bricklayers and materials on a single rail line, builders cannot raise output quickly, so the town's housing supply is likely to be inelastic in the subsidy's first years. The subsidy raises what builders receive per home, but quantity can respond only a little, so much of the early payment may add to builders' earnings on homes they were building anyway. House prices are therefore likely to stay high at first, with extra homes arriving as land, labour and materials expand, if the subsidy lasts.
marking_guidance: The context - the scarce land, the scarce bricklayers and the single rail line - must anchor the answer, and the details of the extract are the evidence.
Reasoning: because a subsidy works through the supply response, the link runs from the town's conditions to how far new houses can follow the higher payment per home.
Conclusion: therefore state what inelastic supply means for the subsidy's first years - higher prices before extra homes, provided the subsidy is sustained.

items.prompt: A stadium in Windhoek holds 10 000 seats. When a local team reaches a cup final there, demand for tickets rises, and the ticket price settles at N$250 instead of the N$100 charged for league games, with all 10 000 seats sold both times. Draw a demand-and-supply diagram of the ticket market to show perfectly inelastic supply and the effect of the rise in demand, and explain what it shows.
items.canonical_answer: Price (N$ a ticket) goes on the vertical axis and tickets on the horizontal. Supply S is a vertical line at 10 000 seats. D1 crosses S at E1, at N$100. The final shifts demand right to D2, which crosses S at E2: N$250 and still 10 000 tickets. The diagram shows perfectly inelastic supply, PES = 0: the rise in demand lands wholly on price, which rises by N$150, while the quantity sold cannot change.
marking_guidance: Axes labelled: price (N$ a ticket) on the vertical axis and quantity (tickets) on the horizontal.
Original curves drawn and labelled: a vertical supply curve S at 10 000 seats, crossed by D1 at E1, N$100.
The shift or movement, in the correct direction: the final shifts demand right from D1 to D2, moving the market up the vertical supply curve.
New equilibrium marked and labelled at E2, N$250 and 10 000 tickets.
What the diagram shows, in words: perfectly inelastic supply, PES = 0, so the change falls wholly on price.
The link between the fixed number of seats and the outcome, and the consequence - a price N$150 higher with no extra tickets sold - carry the analysis marks.

items.prompt: A poultry farmer near Okahandja offers 1 000 eggs a week at N$2 an egg and 1 250 eggs a week at N$2.50. Calculate the price elasticity of supply.
items.canonical_answer: Quantity: 250 / 1000 x 100 = 25 per cent. Price: 0.5 / 2 x 100 = 25 per cent. PES = 25 / 25 = 1, with no units: unit elastic supply, as on a straight-line supply curve through the origin.
marking_guidance: Formula: PES = percentage change in quantity supplied / percentage change in price.
Substitution: 25% / 25%, each change worked on its original level; working that divides the raw changes earns no credit.
Answer with units: 1, a pure number with no units, read as unit elastic.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Price elasticity of supply measures how strongly:
A  the quantity sellers offer responds to a change in the good's price
B  the quantity buyers take responds to a change in the good's price
C  the price responds to a change in the quantity sellers offer
D  sellers' costs respond to a change in the good's price

2. The formula for PES is:
A  percentage change in price / percentage change in quantity supplied
B  percentage change in quantity supplied / percentage change in price
C  change in quantity supplied / change in price, in original units
D  percentage change in quantity supplied x percentage change in price

3. A market's PES works out at 0.4. Supply in this market is:
A  elastic, because the figure is positive
B  elastic, because the figure is below 1
C  inelastic, because the figure is below 1
D  inelastic, because the figure is above 1

4. A price rises by 10% and the quantity supplied rises by 30%. The PES is:
A  3, and supply is elastic
B  3, and supply is inelastic
C  0.33, and supply is elastic
D  20, and supply is elastic

5. Which condition suggests a seller's supply is elastic?
A  its machines run flat out
B  it holds finished goods in store
C  its inputs arrive on one rail line from a single supplier
D  its product takes a season to make

6. For a grain grower, supply is at its least elastic:
A  in the years after new fields are planted
B  in the season in which the crop is already planted
C  in the month after a harvest, with grain in the store
D  in any period in which the price is high

7. On a supply diagram, a steep supply curve shows:
A  quantity offered changing little when price changes
B  quantity offered changing a lot when price changes
C  a market where price changes little
D  a market with no sellers

8. Demand rises in a market whose supply is inelastic. The rise tends to land:
A  on quantity, with little price change
B  on price, with little quantity change
C  on sellers' costs
D  on the government
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 A, 2 B, 3 C, 4 A, 5 B, 6 B, 7 A, 8 B.
1. A measures the seller's side. B is price elasticity of demand - the buyer's response wearing the wrong label; C runs the relationship backwards - quantity follows price here, not price quantity; D confuses elasticity with cost behaviour - PES is silent about costs.
2. B is the formula. A inverts the ratio, which turns every elastic reading inelastic; C drops the percentages, so the figure changes with the units used and cannot be compared across markets; D multiplies, so the figure grows with both changes instead of comparing them.
3. C: a figure below 1 shows the quantity offered changing by a smaller percentage than the price - inelastic. A takes positivity for elasticity, but every PES reading here is positive; B reads the threshold backwards; D misreads the figure itself.
4. A: 30 divided by 10 gives 3, and a figure above 1 is elastic. B pairs the right figure with the wrong reading - the threshold, not the arithmetic, is missed; C inverts the division and then misreads its own threshold; D subtracts the changes instead of dividing them, a percentage-point slip.
5. B: goods in store can be offered at once, so quantity follows price. A leaves no room for output to rise - the inelastic case; C ties inputs to a single source, which delays the response; D means quantity cannot change within the season.
6. B: a planted crop cannot be re-planted mid-season, so the quantity is fixed. A is the period where supply becomes more elastic; C is stocks doing the work - the elastic case; D confuses elasticity with the price level, which are unrelated.
7. A: steepness shows how little the quantity moves for a given price change. B is the flat curve's reading, flipped; C reads the diagram's axes wrongly - price sits on the vertical axis; D abandons the market altogether.
8. B: where quantity cannot follow demand, the adjustment shows up in price. A is what elastic supply would deliver; C sends the adjustment to the wrong party entirely; D names a party the market does not adjust for.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option for each is listed and every distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Each distractor traces to a named confusion: the buyer's elasticity taken for the seller's, the formula inverted, values above and below 1 read backwards, and determinants confused with conditions of demand.

items.prompt:
A radio report from Otavi, March 2026: "Milled maize is dearer in Otavi this month. Namib Grain, the town's big miller, lifted the price of a 12.5 kg bag from N$200 to N$210 and lifted weekly output from 4 000 to 4 400 bags, with a third of its milling line still idle. The village millers around Otavi kept their small hand mills running the same hours as before, and their bag price rose from N$205 to N$230."

Table 1 - milled maize in Otavi, March against February
  Namib Grain price per bag: N$200 in February, N$210 in March
  Namib Grain bags milled a week: 4 000 in February, 4 400 in March
  Namib Grain spare capacity: a third of the milling line idle in both months
  village millers price per bag: N$205 in February, N$230 in March
  village millers bags a week: 900 in February, 910 in March
  village millers working hours: unchanged

(a) Calculate Namib Grain's PES for the price rise. [1]
(b) Identify from Table 1 one reason Namib Grain could raise its output quickly and one reason the village millers could not. [2]
(c) Explain why the village millers' bag price rose further than Namib Grain's. [4]
(d) Analyse what the figures suggest for Otavi's households if demand for milled maize keeps rising. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The formula: PES = percentage change in quantity supplied / percentage change in price. Substitution: bags milled rose by 400 a week, since 4 400 - 4 000 = 400 bags, so the percentage change in quantity supplied is 400 / 4 000 = 10%; the price rose by N$10, since 210 - 200 = N$10, so the percentage change in price is 10 / 200 = 5%. Answer: PES = 10 / 5 = 2, and supply of bags at Namib Grain is elastic, with no units on the figure.
(b) Namib Grain had a third of its milling line idle - spare capacity it could bring into use without new equipment; the village millers kept their hand mills running the same hours, so they had no extra working time to draw on.
(c) The village millers kept their hours the same and milled only 10 more bags a week, since 910 - 900 = 10 bags, against a price rise of N$25, since 230 - 205 = N$25. Their supply is inelastic: hand mills at fixed hours, with no spare capacity in the table, mean the quantity offered cannot follow the price, so when demand for milled maize rose across the district, the shortage showed up in the village millers' price rather than in their output. Namib Grain, with a third of its line idle, met most of the extra demand with extra bags, which kept its price rise to N$10 on a N$200 bag - the smaller price rise sits beside the more elastic supply.
(d) With district demand still rising, output rises where supply is elastic and prices rise where it is not. The table shows this: Namib Grain lifted bags milled by 400 a week on a N$10 price rise, while the village millers lifted output by 10 bags on a N$25 rise. For Otavi's households, extra demand is likely to be met at close to the old price while Namib Grain's idle third lasts; once its line runs flat out, its supply turns inelastic in turn, and further demand lands on price, as the village millers' price already shows. Households near a village miller may switch toward the big miller's cheaper bags, provided the extra demand does not swallow the spare capacity first. However, a good harvest or cheaper imported grain could shift supply right across the district and pull prices back down whatever the elasticities, and the table covers a single month, so seasonal swings in milling may reverse the readings later in the year.

items.prompt:
The market for weekend accommodation in Swakopmund. Answer all parts.

(a) Define price elasticity of supply. [2]
(b) Explain how a figure for price elasticity of supply is calculated and what a figure above 1 shows. [4]
(c) Swakopmund's guesthouses let 2 400 room-nights at N$600 a night before a festival weekend, and 2 520 room-nights at N$900 during it. Analyse what these figures suggest about the elasticity of the town's weekend supply of rooms, and what that meant for festival visitors and guesthouse owners. [6]
(d) Discuss whether an inelastic supply of rooms is good news for a town's guesthouse owners. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Price elasticity of supply measures how strongly the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer responds when the price of the good changes, calculated as the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.
(b) The calculation: PES = the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price, with each percentage worked on the original figure - the change divided by the starting level, times 100. A figure above 1 shows elastic supply: the quantity offered changed by a larger percentage than the price did, so sellers followed the price with room to spare; the higher the figure, the more strongly the quantity responded.
(c) The figures: the quantity of room-nights supplied rose by 120, since 2 520 - 2 400 = 120 room-nights, a rise of 5%, since 120 / 2 400 = 5%, while the nightly price rose by N$300, since 900 - 600 = N$300, a rise of 50%, since 300 / 600 = 50%. PES = 5 / 50 = 0.1, which sits far below 1, so the weekend supply of rooms was inelastic: the quantity of rooms offered could barely follow the price, because rooms are buildings, beds and staff that a weekend cannot add - a short period fixing the quantity, which is the time determinant at work. For festival visitors, the demand rise landed on price - N$300 a night more - while rooms let rose by only 120 room-nights across the town, so visitors paid for the shortage. For the guesthouse owners, the same figures meant a higher rate on almost the same occupancy, so takings usually rose without extra output: the town's fixed room stock decided who gained, with owners taking the revenue and visitors taking the cost.
(d) Why it might be good news: where demand for rooms is rising, inelastic supply means the rise lands on price - owners take N$300 a night more on nearly the same room-nights, so revenue usually rises without the extra costs of beds, staff or buildings, and the shortage itself holds the rate up through the season. Why it might not: the same inelasticity works in reverse - where a downturn empties the town, the price falls on nearly the same fixed costs, and revenue drops sharply because output cannot soften the fall; and in the longer run the high price that inelasticity delivers is an invitation, since new guesthouses and rival towns may draw off the demand the town could not serve, eroding the rate the fixed stock once commanded. Judgement: on balance, inelastic supply is good news for owners while demand rises and the room stock stays fixed, and bad news when demand falls or when the period is long enough for building to answer; whether it pays depends on the direction demand moves and on how long the stock stays fixed.
marking_guidance: Every part carries a model answer; part (d) is level-marked over three bands.
(a) rewards the precise definition: the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.
(b) one mark per distinct point: the formula, the percentage changes worked on the original figures, and what a value above 1 shows.
(c) one mark per distinct linked statement from the figures - the 0.1 reading, the inelastic explanation through the short period, and what each party took.

(d) Level 3 examines why it might - the price rise on a fixed stock while demand rises - and why it might not - the same inelasticity in a downturn, and building answering over time - and reaches a judgement naming the condition; Level 2 develops one side; Level 1 asserts.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "Handmade baskets from the north grow popular in Windhoek shops, and their price rises. The weavers sit in villages with idle hands in the dry season, dyed palm in store, and a craft co-operative that trains new weavers within months. Discuss whether the weavers are likely to gain from the price rise." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for (the weavers gain): elastic supply turns the price rise into income.
Chain 1: popularity rises -> demand shifts right -> the price of a basket rises -> idle hands in the dry season mean spare capacity -> output of baskets rises without much new cost -> weavers' income rises on more baskets (for the weaver, the co-operative).
Case against, first point (the gain leaks away): the weavers sell through Windhoek shops, and the shop owners may keep part of the rise as margin, while buyers may switch to factory-made baskets if the handmade price climbs far.
Chain 2: the shop price rises -> shop margins take part of it -> the weaver's received price rises less than the shop price -> some buyers switch to substitutes -> the volume gain shrinks (for the weaver, the shop owner).
Case against, second point (materials run out): the elastic response may fade, because the stored dyed palm runs low and a fresh palm harvest takes a season.
Chain 3: baskets sell well -> palm stocks empty -> new palm takes a season to harvest -> supply turns inelastic -> the price keeps rising while output stalls (for the weaver, the future buyer).
Judgement: the weavers are likely to gain while spare capacity, stored palm and trained new weavers let output follow the price - an elastic supply meeting rising demand usually means more income on more baskets. The condition the judgement depends on: how much of the shop price reaches the weaver, and whether the stored palm lasts until a new harvest, since the gain holds while the conditions behind supply stay loose enough to answer the demand.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the stated judgement is what is assessed.
The plan must carry the case for and the case against, each developed as a chain from condition to consequence, and name the parties - the weaver, the shop owner, the co-operative.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: the share of the price reaching the weaver, and the stored palm lasting the season.
What settles it: whether supply stays elastic long enough - spare capacity, stocks and new weavers - for the weavers to take the gain in volume rather than hand it to the shops.
